title: A Boy Shoveled My Snow for FREE for 7 Years. 25 Years Later...

scenes.text: Sweetheart, the winter after my husband had his first heart attack, a skinny eleven-year-old boy from the trailer court started shoveling our driveway every time it snowed. Before dawn. Without being asked. And he would never, ever take a penny. For seven winters, I never found out why. And then, twenty-five years later, on the coldest Christmas Eve in Ohio history, he came back, and he told me.
scenes.query: boy shoveling snowy driveway before dawn
scenes.caption: HE NEVER TOOK A PENNY

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you about that boy, the one time I caught him, and the secret he'd been keeping since nineteen eighty-nine. Stay with me, honey, because the reason he shoveled my driveway is something I had done and completely forgotten. And it's the reason I believe nothing kind you ever do is wasted.
scenes.query: elderly woman at frosty window looking out
scenes.caption: SOMETHING I'D FORGOTTEN

scenes.text: In the fall of nineteen eighty-nine, Harold had a heart attack at the plant. He was only forty-seven, but he'd smoked for thirty years. He came home from the hospital with a bottle of pills and strict orders from the doctor. No smoking. No red meat. And no shoveling snow. Not one shovelful, the doctor said. Shoveling snow kills more men with bad hearts every winter than anything else.
scenes.query: man in hospital bed 1980s wife beside him
scenes.caption: NO SHOVELING SNOW

scenes.text: Now, Harold was a stubborn man, honey. The first time it snowed that December, I woke up at five in the morning to the sound of a shovel scraping on the driveway. And I flew out of bed, ready to kill him. But Harold was right there next to me, snoring. Somebody else was out there in the dark, shoveling our driveway. In a minute I'll tell you who.
scenes.query: woman looking out bedroom window at dawn snow
scenes.caption: SOMEBODY WAS OUT THERE

scenes.text: I ran to the window. And there, in the light from the streetlamp, was a little figure in a too-big coat and a knit cap, shoveling as fast as he could. By the time I got my robe on and opened the front door, he was gone. Running down the street toward the trailer court on Leppo Road. Our driveway was clean, honey. Every inch. Even the front walk.
scenes.query: small figure shoveling under streetlamp
scenes.caption: HE WAS GONE

scenes.text: It happened every time it snowed that winter. Every single time. Five in the morning, the scrape of the shovel, and by the time I got to the door, he was gone. Harold was mortified. He said, Ruthie, I'm not a charity case. Find out who it is and pay him. So I left five dollars in an envelope taped to the mailbox, with a note that said, thank you, please take this.
scenes.query: envelope taped to mailbox in snow
scenes.caption: PLEASE TAKE THIS

scenes.text: The next morning, the driveway was shoveled, and the envelope was still on the mailbox. With the five dollars inside. And under my note, in a child's pencil handwriting, it said, no thank you. And that was it, honey. Every winter after that, the same. I tried leaving cookies. Gone. Hot cocoa in a thermos. Gone, and the thermos washed and left on the porch. But money, never.
scenes.query: child's pencil handwriting no thank you
scenes.caption: NO THANK YOU

scenes.text: If you're enjoying Grandma's story, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. One morning in the second winter, I hid behind the front door at four thirty with my coat on, and when I heard the shovel, I flung it open. And there he was, finally. A skinny boy with big brown eyes and a scar on his chin. He froze like a deer.
scenes.query: boy frozen with shovel caught in porch light
scenes.caption: HE FROZE LIKE A DEER

scenes.text: I said, honey, who are you? Why are you doing this? And he said, my name's Tony, ma'am. And then he said, I just like shoveling. Which was the worst lie I've ever heard in my life. Nobody likes shoveling at five in the morning when it's ten degrees. I said, Tony, at least come in and have some breakfast. And he shook his head and ran off.
scenes.query: boy running away down snowy street
scenes.caption: I JUST LIKE SHOVELING

scenes.text: So I asked around. Tony Russo. He lived in the trailer court on Leppo Road with his grandmother. His mother was gone, nobody knew where. His father was in prison in Mansfield, the big reformatory. He was a quiet kid, the school said. Smart. A little wild. Got in fights sometimes when the other boys teased him about his father. And he walked a mile each way in the snow to shovel our driveway.
scenes.query: trailer court in winter small town
scenes.caption: TONY RUSSO

scenes.text: For seven winters, honey. From eleven to eighteen. Through Harold's second heart attack, and my mother's funeral, and the blizzard of ninety-four. Every snowfall, before dawn, without fail. Harold stopped being mortified after the first year. He'd lie in bed and listen to that shovel and say, there's our boy. And then, the winter Tony turned eighteen, the scraping stopped. He'd joined the Navy.
scenes.query: young man in navy uniform at bus station
scenes.caption: THERE'S OUR BOY

scenes.text: Before he left for the Navy, honey, I did one thing. I knitted him a scarf, navy blue, and I put it in a box with a note and a hundred dollars from our savings, and I took it to his grandmother's trailer. She came to the door, a tiny woman with a cane. She took the scarf and the note. But she handed me back the money. She said, he told me you'd try this. He said to tell you no thank you.
scenes.query: elderly woman at trailer door with cane
scenes.caption: HE SAID NO THANK YOU

scenes.text: So far, the heart attack, the envelope, and the boy with the scar. We never heard from Tony after that, sweetheart. Harold passed in two thousand eight. I wondered about Tony every winter, every time I heard a neighbor shoveling. Was he alive? Was he all right? Did he make it out of that trailer court? I prayed for him. And I never, ever figured out why he'd done it.
scenes.query: elderly woman praying by snowy window
scenes.caption: WHY HAD HE DONE IT?

scenes.text: Christmas Eve, two thousand fourteen. It was nine below zero, the coldest Christmas Eve anyone in Ohio could remember. And at five o'clock in the morning, I woke up in my bed, seventy years old, to a sound I hadn't heard in twenty years. The scrape of a shovel on my driveway. And I lay there, and I thought I was dreaming, honey. I thought it was Harold's ghost.
scenes.query: elderly woman awake in bed at dawn listening
scenes.caption: THE SCRAPE OF A SHOVEL

scenes.text: I put on my robe and went to the door, and opened it. And there in the streetlight, shoveling my driveway, was a big man in a Navy peacoat, with gray at his temples. He stopped and turned around. He had a scar on his chin. And he said, morning, Mrs. Miller. I heard you've been doing your own driveway since Mr. Miller passed. That's not right. And he smiled.
scenes.query: man in navy peacoat with shovel at dawn
scenes.caption: MORNING, MRS. MILLER

scenes.text: I made him come in this time, sweetheart. I didn't give him a choice. I sat him down in Harold's chair in my kitchen with a cup of coffee and a plate of eggs, and I said, Tony Russo, you are going to tell me why, right now, or I'm calling the police. And he laughed, and then he got very quiet, and he took out his wallet, and he unfolded a little piece of paper.
scenes.query: man taking folded paper from wallet
scenes.caption: TELL ME WHY

scenes.text: It was a note, honey. Old, soft, falling apart. And it was in my handwriting. It said, To the little boy at the bus stop. Your daddy made a mistake. That doesn't make you one. You are a good boy. Merry Christmas. And taped to it was a two-dollar bill. I'd completely forgotten it, sweetheart. I stared at my own handwriting and couldn't remember writing it.
scenes.query: old handwritten note with two dollar bill
scenes.caption: YOU ARE A GOOD BOY

scenes.text: Tony told me. In December of nineteen eighty-eight, when he was ten, a group of boys at the bus stop by the five-and-dime were teasing him about his father being in prison. They pushed him down in the slush. And a lady in a red coat, waiting for the bus, chased them off with her umbrella. She gave him a tissue for his bloody chin. And before she got on her bus, she pressed that note into his hand.
scenes.query: woman in red coat chasing boys with umbrella
scenes.caption: THE LADY IN RED

scenes.text: I remembered it then, honey. Barely. I'd written it on the back of a grocery list, on the bus, with a little two-dollar bill from my coin purse. I'd never seen the boy again. Tony said, Mrs. Miller, I read that note every night for a year. Everybody else said I'd end up like my dad. You were the only person who ever said I was good. And then I saw your name on the mailbox. And your husband was sick.
scenes.query: boy reading note by flashlight in bed
scenes.caption: THE ONLY ONE

scenes.text: Harold knew, sweetheart. That's the other thing Tony told me. One morning in the third winter, Harold had gotten up at five, without telling me, and gone out on the porch in his bathrobe, and caught Tony. And Tony told him the whole story. And Harold made him promise to keep shoveling, and never to tell me. He said, let her wonder. It'll do her good to get something she can't pay back.
scenes.query: old man on porch in bathrobe talking to boy
scenes.caption: HAROLD KNEW

scenes.text: Harold kept that secret for eighteen years, honey, until the day he died. My Harold, who couldn't keep a surprise party secret for two days. I sat at that kitchen table and laughed and cried at the same time. Tony said, Mr. Miller used to bring me a cup of coffee on the porch every morning, before your cocoa. Black, with one sugar. He got up at four thirty to make it.
scenes.query: cup of hot cocoa on snowy porch rail
scenes.caption: HE GOT UP AT FOUR THIRTY

scenes.text: Tony spent twenty years in the Navy, sweetheart. He became a chief petty officer. When he got out, he went to school and became a counselor, at a juvenile detention center in Columbus. For boys whose fathers are in prison. Boys exactly like he was. He said, I tell every one of them the same thing you told me. Your daddy made a mistake. That doesn't make you one.
scenes.query: counselor talking with teenage boys
scenes.caption: THAT DOESN'T MAKE YOU ONE

scenes.text: And then he told me why he'd come back that particular Christmas. His own father had just died, in prison, the month before. Tony had gone to see him at the end, for the first time in thirty years, and forgiven him. And on the drive home, he said, he thought of me, and the shovel, and Harold. And he couldn't stand the thought of me shoveling my own driveway at seventy.
scenes.query: man driving alone on winter highway thinking
scenes.caption: HE FORGAVE HIM

scenes.text: Tony lives in Mansfield now, honey, ten minutes away. He's married, with two boys. And every time it snows, at five in the morning, I hear the scrape of a shovel. Now it's his boys doing it, and Tony supervising with a cup of my coffee. They never take a penny either. I've stopped trying. Some debts, you just have to let people pay.
scenes.query: father and two boys shoveling driveway dawn
scenes.caption: THEY NEVER TAKE A PENNY

scenes.text: Here's what I want you to remember, sweetheart. I spent two dollars and thirty seconds on a crying boy at a bus stop, and I forgot about it by the time I got home. He carried it for twenty-six years. You never know which kindness will be the one. Tell me in the comments, honey, has a stranger's words ever changed your life? There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night.
scenes.query: snowy driveway shoveled clean at sunrise
scenes.caption: TWO DOLLARS AND THIRTY SECONDS
